AlternateTargets: make a meal by steaming sand
Senses.Note: The literal impossible operation and its proverbial use remain one sense because every sampled deployment preserves sand, steaming, and failed rice-making. The later claim that everyone can be fed is an inversion of the same fixed image, not a new referent. The entry preserves that reversal without deciding whether the praise is sincere or ironic.

Occurrences.Kwic: 向外馳求，以至盲修瞎煉，如蒸砂作飯，終不成事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (費隱禪師語錄), hall address. Feiyin Tongrong is the exact speaker: in his own discussion following a question about the monastery setting, he compares outward seeking and blind refining to steaming sand to make rice.

Occurrences.Kwic: 譬如蒸砂作飯，豈療飢瘡？掘地覓天，莫覩霄漢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chijue Daochong (痴絕道冲禪師語錄). Chijue Daochong is the exact speaker of the uninterrupted instruction: he compares intentional investigation and verbal theorizing to steaming sand to make rice and digging into earth to seek heaven.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：談玄說妙，𦘕餅充飢；舉古論今，蒸砂作飯。去此二途，如何通信？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Jieshi Zhipeng (介石智朋禪師語錄), an ascent-seat exchange. The exact headword-bearing speaker is an unnamed questioning monk, who contrasts discussing past and present as making rice by steaming sand and asks how to communicate beyond two failed routes. All six attribution rungs leave this monk without a personal name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喝水成冰，法法森嚴，蒸砂作飯，人人可飽，非堂頭法兄，安能大暢宗猷、光斯盛業？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (蔗菴範禪師語錄). Zhean Jingfan is the exact actor: his (東塔) address says (蒸砂作飯)，(人人可飽).

SearchAliases: make a meal by steaming sand
Zen steam sand to make rice
Senses.Explanation: The records state the failure inside the comparison. One says that seeking outside and blind refining are "like steaming sand to make rice: in the end the matter is not accomplished" (如蒸砂作飯，終不成事). Another asks whether steaming sand to make rice could cure the sore of hunger (譬如蒸砂作飯，豈療飢瘡). It also appears in public interview: an unnamed monk contrasts talking mystery and discussing the old with two futile attempts at nourishment, then asks how a message is passed apart from those roads. One later address by Zhean Jingfan deliberately reverses the fixed impossibility—"steam sand to make rice; everyone can be fed" (蒸砂作飯，人人可飽)—inside praise of the addressed teacher. The Zen corpus therefore uses the impossible meal as criticism, paired proverb, interview premise, and marked inversion.
